extracted.intended_audience: students learning introductory calculus (advanced high-school or undergraduate)
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook-style chapter setting out foundational definitions, rules, techniques and geometric/physical interpretations for integration and differentiation (Riemann sums, linearity, power rule, product/quotient rules, trig derivatives, extrema, etc.). Useful for learning, teaching, or checking standard calculus methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral defined as limit of finite sums (Riemann sum / area)
rubrics_metrics.description: The integral ∫_a^b f(x) dx is understood as an area and defined as the limit of finite sums (definition (5)): S_n = Σ f(x_i) Δx_i as the partition gets finer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by simple examples (constant functions produce rectangles whose Riemann sums are trivial). Emphasizes interpreting integrals geometrically as areas and computing them by passing to the limit of sums; caution about limits when numerator and denominator both tend to zero. Exercises ask the reader to reproduce limits for x^k and other functions using this definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linearity of the integral (additivity and scalar multiplication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formula (9): ∫_a^b [c f(x) + d g(x)] dx = c ∫_a^b f(x) dx + d ∫_a^b g(x) dx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof follows immediately from the definition (limit of sums). Extends to sums of more than two functions. Used to integrate polynomials termwise; examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power rule for integrals (integration of x^n)
rubrics_metrics.description: For integer k (and extended to rational k by limiting arguments), ∫_a^b x^k dx = (b^{k+1} - a^{k+1})/(k+1) (formula (7) and discussion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by evaluation of limits in the Riemann-sum model; exercises ask to check special rational and negative cases and to derive limits from sums. The text shows how special-case computations led historically to the general rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of variable / shift in integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of the integral does not depend on the name of the integration variable; shifting coordinates: ∫_a^b f(x) dx = ∫_{a'}^{b'} f(1+u) du (example formula (12)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained geometrically by shifting the origin; concrete examples (12a–12d) show substitution x = 1 + u and how it affects limits; used to transform integrals like ∫ x^k dx via substitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral sign reversal and zero-length interval
rubrics_metrics.description: If the bounds are equal the integral is zero; and ∫_a^b f(x) dx = -∫_b^a f(x) dx (rule (11) and discussion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from the definition and geometric interpretation (area with zero base). Used implicitly in manipulation of integrals and change-of-variable formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of integrals (monotonicity and bounding)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f(x) ≤ g(x) on [a,b] then ∫_a^b f(x) dx ≤ ∫_a^b g(x) dx (formula (13)); in particular, if f(x) ≤ M then ∫_a^b f(x) dx ≤ M(b-a) (formula (14)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained both by geometric area comparison and by analytic Riemann-sum argument. Used to obtain rough but useful bounds and to compare integrals in exercises (e.g., bounding ∫_0^1 x^n sin x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute-value inequality for integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: Inequality |∫_a^b f(x) dx| ≤ ∫_a^b |f(x)| dx (formula (16)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from comparison with |f(x)| and the observation that -∫|f| ≤ ∫ f ≤ ∫ |f|. Useful for estimating integrals and proving convergence/estimates in exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret integrals via symmetry and geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpreting definite integrals as areas under curves and using symmetry properties of integrands to evaluate integrals (hint sections for trigonometric integrals and odd/even functions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises encourage considering graphs and symmetry with respect to x=0 to evaluate integrals (e.g., integrals of sin and cos over symmetric intervals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative as slope of tangent (geometric definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: By definition, the derivative f'(x) is the slope of the tangent to the curve y = f(x) at x, obtained as the limit of slopes of secant lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains tangent approximated by secant lines P P_i and defines slope of secant as difference quotient Δy/Δx; the tangent slope is the limit as Δx → 0. Visual figures and geometric intuition are emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative as a limit / difference quotient
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition (1): f'(x) = lim_{x_i → x} [f(x_i) - f(x)]/(x_i - x) (equivalently lim_{h→0} [f(x+h)-f(x)]/h).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as the fundamental limiting operation of differentiation; alternative notations Df(x) and dy/dx introduced. Text gives worked examples showing algebraic simplification of difference quotients to remove 0/0 indeterminacy before taking limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiability implies continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: If the derivative f'(x) exists at a point, then f is continuous at that point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short theoretical remark: existence of limit of Δy/Δx implies Δy → 0 as Δx → 0. The book omits repetitive continuity proofs for differentiable functions unless special reasons arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power rule for derivatives (integer and rational exponents)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f(x) = x^n (n a positive integer), f'(x) = n x^{n-1}; extended: for any positive or negative rational r, derivative of x^r is r x^{r-1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example computations use algebraic factorization to cancel (x_i - x) and pass to the limit; exercises ask to prove the statement for integer n by induction and extend to rational exponents via inverse and chain/inverse-function reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic differentiation rules: sum, product, quotient
rubrics_metrics.description: Sum rule: derivative of sum is sum of derivatives. Product rule: (fg)' = f g' + g f'. Quotient rule: (f/g)' = (g f' - f g')/g^2 (assuming g ≠ 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Product rule is proved by adding and subtracting the same term and taking limits; quotient rule left as exercise. These rules provide an algorithmic toolkit to differentiate polynomials, rational functions and many standard forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiation of inverse functions
rubrics_metrics.description: If y=f(x) and x=g(y) are inverses, then g'(y) = 1 / f'(x) (or Dg(y) = 1/Df(x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained via reciprocal difference quotients and geometrically by swapping axes. Examples include x = y^m and y = x^{1/m}, and the inverse trigonometric example y = arctan x (with domain restrictions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivatives of trigonometric functions (use radian measure)
rubrics_metrics.description: D sin x = cos x; D cos x = -sin x; D tan x = 1/cos^2 x (and similarly for cot, sec, csc). Radian measure must be used for these differentiation formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivations use trig addition formulas and limits lim_{h→0} sin h / h = 1, lim_{h→0} (cos h - 1)/h = 0. The text emphasizes exclusive use of radian measure when differentiating trig functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: algebraic simplification of difference quotients
rubrics_metrics.description: When direct substitution in the difference quotient yields 0/0, algebraic rearrangement (factorization, cancellation) should be used to remove the common factor (x_i - x) before taking the limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple worked examples (powers, square roots, rational functions) show cancellation techniques leading to continuous expressions whose limits can be evaluated by substitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second derivative: concavity and inflection
rubrics_metrics.description: The sign of the second derivative f''(x) indicates concavity: f''>0 concave upward, f''<0 concave downward; f''=0 often indicates an inflection point where concavity changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains geometric meaning (curve bending), gives examples (parabola x^2 concave up, x^3 has inflection at 0), and mentions curvature k expressible via first and second derivatives (formula referenced without proof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding extrema via first and second derivatives
rubrics_metrics.description: To find maxima and minima: compute f'(x), solve f'(x)=0 for critical points, then use second derivative f''(x) (sign test) to classify roots as maxima (f''<0) or minima (f''>0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked polynomial example (2x^3 - 9x^2 + 12x + 1) demonstrates finding roots of f' and classifying via f''. Exercises include many extremum problems and sketching graphs showing intervals of increase/decrease and concavity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical interpretation: derivative as instantaneous rate (velocity) and second derivative as acceleration
rubrics_metrics.description: If position x=f(t) depends on time t, then instantaneous velocity is v=f'(t) (limit of average velocities) and acceleration is a=f''(t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton's viewpoint is presented; Galileo's freely falling body x=(1/2) g t^2 is used as example to compute v = g t and constant acceleration a = g. Exercises ask for trajectories for parametric plane motions and times/positions of extrema in motion problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique and pedagogy: differentiation/integration as algorithmic procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical note and pedagogical warning: calculus developed general rules that allow mechanical/algorithmic solution of many problems; however, overemphasis on mechanics can degrade teaching into empty drill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages mastery of a few simple rules and recognition of applicability; includes both mechanical rule lists and geometric/physical interpretations to maintain conceptual understanding.
